prompt: A job has `environment: prod`, and the `prod` environment has a required-reviewer protection rule configured in repo settings. What actually happens when that job is reached?
choices: The job runs immediately and sends a notification to the reviewer afterward
The job's steps pause and do not execute until a listed reviewer approves it in the Review deployments panel
The job is skipped silently because no reviewer responded within the run
The protection rule only affects which secrets are visible, not when the job runs

prompt: In a correct dev -> staging -> prod promotion pipeline, where should the `staging` and `prod` deploy jobs get the artifact tag to deploy?
choices: Each job should rebuild the image fresh from the current main branch to make sure it's up to date
Each job should deploy whatever tag is currently pushed as :latest in the registry
Each job should reference the exact tag produced once by the build job, e.g. via needs.build.outputs.image_tag
Each job should read the tag from a hardcoded value typed into that job's YAML

prompt: What is the actual traffic-switching mechanism in a blue-green deploy, as opposed to a canary deploy?
choices: Blue-green gradually increases the percentage of traffic to the new version over several steps; canary flips a single switch and moves 100% at once

Blue-green flips a single routing target (e.g. a Service selector or load-balancer target group) so 100% of traffic moves at once; canary gradually increases the percentage of traffic to the new version over several steps
Both strategies use the exact same weighted-routing mechanism, just with different names
Blue-green only applies to databases; canary only applies to stateless web services

prompt: A canary rollout is paused at setWeight: 10 when the new version starts throwing errors. What is the actual blast radius at that moment, compared to a blue-green cutover that had the same bug?
choices: Identical: both strategies expose 100% of users to the bug immediately
Canary exposes roughly 10% of traffic to the bug and can abort back to stable; blue-green would have already exposed 100% of traffic the instant it cut over
Canary exposes 100% of traffic because weight settings don't actually affect live requests
Blue-green is unaffected because it doesn't use real production traffic

prompt: A team removes a field from an existing API response that other services depend on. Following semantic versioning, what kind of version bump is this?
choices: PATCH, since it's a small change
MINOR, since no new dependency was added
MAJOR, since it can break existing clients
No version bump is needed since the endpoint URL didn't change

prompt: Beyond the mutable-pointer problem already covered for a single deploy, why specifically is `:latest` wrong for an artifact moving through a dev -> staging -> prod promotion pipeline?
choices: latest tags are not supported by any container registry
latest images are always larger in size than semver-tagged images
If a new build pushes over :latest while an earlier build is still being promoted, prod could deploy bits that were never actually validated in staging
latest tags cannot be pulled by Kubernetes, only by Docker Compose

prompt: A workflow-file PR changes a job's trigger from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` and adds `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` to its checkout step, in the same job that references a repository secret. Why should a reviewer treat this as a serious security finding?
choices: It has no real effect; pull_request_target behaves identically to pull_request in all cases
It only affects billing for Actions minutes, not security
It runs the fork PR's own (attacker-controlled) code in a context that now has access to the base repo's secrets, letting any contributor exfiltrate them via a PR
It disables all secrets for the workflow, making the job strictly safer

prompt: What is the purpose of adding a CODEOWNERS entry for `/.github/workflows/`?
choices: It automatically fixes any syntax errors in workflow YAML before merge
It speeds up the Actions runner by skipping steps the owning team marks as optional
It requires sign-off from the designated team before a change to pipeline files can be merged, since those files control deploys and hold secret references
It prevents the workflow from ever being triggered by pull requests
